input:
Staff Data Platform Engineer, Data Governance
Woodgrove - Remote, United States

Woodgrove builds the claims and payments data platform that regional insurers use to settle member claims, reconcile provider payments, and answer regulator questions. Nine carriers and more than four hundred provider groups send records through it every day. The data platform group is fourteen engineers split across ingestion, governance, and warehouse teams, and it sits beside a compliance office that reviews every change to a regulated field before release.

This staff role joins the governance team. You will set the standards that producing teams follow when they publish a new feed, review the contracts that bind those feeds to their consumers, and help the warehouse team keep reporting tables stable while upstream systems change underneath them. The team ships in small increments, writes design notes before large changes, and treats a broken downstream report as its own incident.

What you will do:
- Run the streaming ingestion tier that carries claims, eligibility, and payment events from carriers into the platform.
- Set the compatibility rules every published schema must pass, and review proposed breaking changes with the teams that own them.
- Write and review data quality rules, and make sure each failure reaches the team that can fix it.
- Keep lineage current from regulator-facing reports back to the carrier feeds that produced them.
- Model warehouse tables for analysts, actuaries, and the compliance office, and keep load windows short.
- Replace remaining manual reconciliation work with scheduled, observable jobs.
- Write design notes, take part in architecture reviews, and share an on-call rotation with the platform group.

Requirements:
- Design and operate streaming ingestion pipelines on Kafka.
- Write production Python services for data pipelines.
- Provision cloud infrastructure as code with Terraform.
- Design schema governance and compatibility rules for shared data contracts.
- Build data quality rules owned by the teams that produce the data.
- Trace data lineage from published reports back to source systems.
- Model analytical warehouses in PostgreSQL.
- 8+ years of professional data engineering experience.
- Experience with regulated data, such as health or insurance records.
- Automate manual reconciliation and reporting processes.
- Partner with compliance and analytics teams on data definitions.
- Authorized to work in the United States without sponsorship.

Nice to have:
- Experience with Go.
- Experience with Kubernetes.
- Familiarity with dbt.
- Experience with Apache Spark.
- Experience with a workflow orchestrator such as Airflow or Dagster.
- Containerize services with Docker.
- Run CI/CD pipelines in GitHub Actions.
- Manage secrets with Vault.
- Experience with Snowflake.
- Metadata cataloging experience.
- Dimensional modeling for reporting workloads.
- Mentor engineers through design reviews.
- Experience with AI-assisted coding tools.
- Reduce pipeline latency for high-volume feeds.
- On-call experience for a data platform.
- Experience with AWS.
- Negotiate data contracts between producer and consumer teams.
- Explain technical tradeoffs clearly in writing.


About the team:
The governance team is four engineers and a product manager. Two of the engineers came from carrier systems, one from the warehouse team, and one from a hospital data group. The team owns the schema standards document, the contract review queue, the quality rule library, and the lineage service. It holds a short planning meeting on Mondays, a design review on Wednesdays, and keeps the rest of the week for focused work.

In your first ninety days you will take over the contract review queue, ship one change to the compatibility rules after a design note and review, and pair with the warehouse team on a reporting model that depends on a feed your team governs. By the end of your first year we expect you to have set the direction for how the platform handles a breaking change that cannot be avoided, from the first notice to consumers through the cutover and the retirement of the old field.

Our stack:
Kafka for streaming, PostgreSQL for the warehouse and the metadata store, Python for services and jobs, Go for two latency-sensitive connectors, Terraform for every environment, Vault for secrets, Docker and GitHub Actions for builds and deployment. We are evaluating a managed orchestration service for scheduled jobs and expect to decide during the next two quarters.

Interview process:
A thirty-minute call with the hiring manager, a take-home design note on a schema change problem that we pay you for, a ninety-minute review of that note with two engineers, and a final conversation with the compliance lead and the head of the platform group. We aim to finish within three weeks and will tell you where you stand after each step.

Compensation:
The base salary range for this role is set by level and published to candidates at the first call. It is paired with an annual bonus target and an equity grant that vests over four years.

How we work:
Woodgrove is remote-first across the United States, with two in-person planning weeks a year. Engineers own their services from design through operation. We publish salary ranges internally, review them every year, and expect people to take their full leave.

Benefits:
- Medical, dental, and vision coverage for you and your dependents.
- A retirement plan with an employer match.
- Sixteen weeks of paid parental leave.
- A yearly learning budget and a home office stipend.

Woodgrove is an equal opportunity employer. We consider every qualified applicant without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, disability, or veteran status. If you need an accommodation during the interview process, tell your recruiter and we will arrange it.

research.text:
Engineering at Woodgrove. Woodgrove started as a claims clearinghouse for three regional insurers and now runs the data platform that nine carriers rely on to settle claims and pay providers. Every record that moves through the platform can end up in front of a state regulator, so the engineering group treats traceability as a product feature rather than an audit chore. A figure on a regulator report should lead back, in a few clicks, to the carrier feed and the exact file that produced it.

The platform group is organized into three teams. Ingestion owns the connectors that receive carrier and provider files and the streaming tier that turns them into events. Governance owns the schema standards, the contract reviews between producers and consumers, and the quality rules that guard regulated fields. Warehouse owns the reporting models that actuaries, analysts, and the compliance office query every day. The teams share an architecture review each week and a single on-call rotation, so an engineer on any team learns how the other two work.

We write before we build. A change that touches more than one team starts as a short design note that names the problem, the options considered, and how the change will be rolled back. Notes are reviewed in the open, and anyone in the company can comment. Most notes are two pages; the longest ones are about migrations, because a migration that goes wrong in this domain can delay a provider payment.

Quality rules belong to the people who can act on them. When a rule fails, the alert goes to the team that produces the column, not to a shared channel that nobody reads. Governance reviews rule coverage every quarter with each producing team and publishes the coverage figures to the whole company.

We hire for judgment more than for any particular tool. The platform runs on Kafka, PostgreSQL, Python, and Terraform today, and it will run on something else in five years. What we look for is someone who can explain why a design choice fits a regulated setting, who notices when a fix hides a symptom, and who leaves a system easier for the next engineer to change.

Woodgrove engineers work remotely from across the United States. We meet in person twice a year to plan, and most teams keep a few overlapping hours each day for pairing and review. New engineers spend their first month shadowing on-call and shipping one small change through every stage of review, so they see the whole path before they own a service.

Our compliance office is part of engineering planning, not a gate at the end. Its analysts sit in design reviews for any change to a regulated field, and they help engineers read new state rules as they are published. That partnership is why a regulator question can usually be answered the same day it arrives.

A recent example shows how the teams work together. Last spring a carrier announced it would split one claim status field into two, effective at the start of the next quarter. Governance wrote the design note the same week, listing every report and model that read the old field. Warehouse built the new models beside the old ones, and ingestion ran both feeds in parallel for a month while the compliance office compared the regulator reports produced each way. The old field was retired two weeks after the carrier's date, with no late report and no manual correction.

We measure ourselves by what our users can do without us. Analysts should be able to find where a column comes from without asking an engineer. Producing teams should be able to publish a compatible change without waiting for a review slot. The compliance office should be able to answer a regulator from the lineage service alone. Each quarter we pick the request we hear most often and remove the reason for it.

Engineers here grow by taking on wider problems rather than by moving into management by default. Staff and principal engineers set direction across teams, write the hardest design notes, and review the rest. Managers own hiring, growth, and staffing. Both paths have the same levels and the same pay bands, and people move between them.

We keep a public engineering handbook. It explains how on-call works, how incidents are reviewed, how design notes are written, and how we decide to retire a system. New engineers are asked to fix one thing in it during their first month, because a handbook nobody edits stops describing how the team actually works.

My data quality rules cover 1,400 columns, and a failure goes to the team that owns the column rather than to a shared inbox. I also contributed to a lineage service that follows any column to its source system, which four downstream teams adopted.
Woodgrove settles claims for nine carriers, and a figure on a regulator report has to lead back to the carrier file behind it. Its alerts go to the teams that produce each column.

Before that I modeled a clinical reporting warehouse in PostgreSQL and brought its nightly load from 7 hours to 95 minutes. I automated a reconciliation process that had taken two analyst days a week, and my Terraform modules replaced a two-day runbook for provisioning each environment.

input:
Principal Data Engineer, Governance
Litware - Remote or Lakeshore, Ohio

Litware runs the scheduling and records platform behind more than two hundred outpatient clinics. Clinic staff use it to book visits, record procedures, and send claims, and the data group turns those records into the operational and financial reporting that clinic owners and their auditors read each month.

This principal role leads data governance across the group's three pipelines. You will decide how producing teams publish schemas, how quality failures are routed, and how a figure on a monthly report is traced back to the visit that produced it. You will also work closely with the clinical analytics team, whose metric definitions drive what the pipelines compute.

What you will do:
- Own the event streaming pipelines that carry visit, procedure, and claim events from clinic systems.
- Set schema registry policy and review compatibility exceptions with each producing team.
- Build quality checks for regulated fields and route each failure to an accountable owner.
- Extend column-level lineage so analysts can trace any reported figure to its source records.
- Shorten warehouse load windows and make failed steps resumable.
- Retire the remaining spreadsheet reports that clinic owners still receive by email.
- Mentor senior engineers and represent the data group in architecture reviews.

Requirements:
- Build and run event streaming pipelines on Kafka for operational data.
- Own schema registry design and compatibility policy across producing teams.
- Implement data quality checks that route failures to accountable owners.
- Write and maintain production Python for batch and streaming jobs.

research.text:
Data at Litware. Outpatient clinics run on narrow margins and tight schedules, and the owners we serve want to know by the morning what happened in their clinics the day before. The data group exists to give them that answer, and to give their auditors the same answer with every step shown.

We run three pipelines. The visit pipeline carries bookings, check-ins, and procedures from clinic systems as events. The claims pipeline turns those procedures into claims and follows each one through payment or denial. The reporting pipeline builds the warehouse that clinic owners, finance staff, and our clinical analytics team read. Each pipeline has its own team, and a governance lead sets the rules all three follow.

Schemas are a shared contract. A team that wants to change a published event writes up the change, checks it against the registry's compatibility rules, and talks to every consumer before it ships. Exceptions are rare and recorded. When a breaking change does reach production, the team that shipped it writes the incident review, even if another team found the problem first.

Every regulated field has an owner and a quality check. A failed check pages the owning team during working hours and opens a ticket outside them. Clinic owners never see a figure that failed a check without a note explaining what was wrong and when it will be corrected.

Our clinical analytics team decides what a metric means. Data engineers sit with those analysts when a new metric is defined, because a definition that cannot be computed from the records we hold is a definition we should not publish. That conversation happens before any pipeline work begins.

We value engineers who simplify. The best change we shipped last year deleted a nightly job that copied a table nobody read. We would rather run fewer systems well than many systems badly, and we review our own platform for things to retire every quarter.

Litware has engineers in eleven states. Most work remotely, and a smaller group works from our Lakeshore office, where the clinical analytics team is based. We gather once a year to plan, and the rest of our collaboration happens in design notes, reviews, and pairing sessions during shared core hours.

What a week looks like. Monday starts with a short review of the weekend's quality checks and any figure that went out with a correction note. Tuesday and Thursday are kept free of meetings for focused work. Wednesday holds the cross-team design review, where any engineer can bring a note. Friday afternoon is for retiring something: a job, a table, a dashboard, or a check that no longer guards anything.

Last year the claims team moved its pipeline from nightly batches to events. Clinic owners used to see yesterday's denials at noon; now they see them as the payer sends them. The move took two quarters, ran old and new paths side by side for six weeks, and ended with an incident review of the one day the two paths disagreed, which turned out to be a time zone error in the old path that had been there for years.

Our auditors are users too. Clinic owners hand our monthly reports to outside auditors, and those auditors ask how a figure was computed. We give them a lineage view that starts at the figure and ends at the visits behind it, and we answer their questions within two business days. Extending that view from the reporting pipeline to the claims and visit pipelines is the most requested change on our roadmap.

We hire people who explain their reasoning. In review we ask why a change is shaped the way it is, what else was considered, and how it will be undone if it goes wrong. Good answers are short and specific. Nobody is expected to know every tool we run, and everyone is expected to say when they do not know something.

Growth at Litware does not require managing people. Senior, staff, and principal engineers lead through design notes, reviews, and mentoring, and they are paid on the same bands as managers at the same level.

paragraphs.text: Quality rules I introduced now guard 1,900 columns, and each failure is routed to the producing team. With two colleagues I designed a schema registry whose compatibility rules caught 31 breaking changes before release.
Litware gives clinic owners a morning view of the day before, and every regulated field in its pipelines has an owner and a check.

At a health system I modeled the clinical reporting warehouse in PostgreSQL and cut its nightly load from 7 hours to 95 minutes. I rewrote the load orchestration in Python so a failed step resumed on its own instead of replaying the night.

Earlier I delivered the first automated reporting pipeline for a freight brokerage, retiring spreadsheets that circulated by email. More recently my Kafka ingestion rebuild took median latency from 40 minutes to 90 seconds.
